at danse.explanation: "At danse" means "to dance": "Vil du danse?" (Do you want to dance?). To say who with, use "med" (with): "Jeg danser med Anna" (I dance with Anna).

sentence.da: Der er musik, og jeg vil **danse** med dig.
sentence.en: There is music, and I want to dance with you.

at dele.explanation: "At dele" means "to share" and also "to divide". In maths it means divide: "ti delt med to" (ten divided by two).

sentence.da: Vi vil **dele** en pizza, så vi får en halv hver.
sentence.en: We want to share a pizza, so we each get half.

at drikke.explanation: "At drikke" means "to drink", for water, coffee, beer and so on: "Jeg drikker kaffe" (I drink coffee).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **drikke** et glas koldt vand, for jeg er tørstig.
sentence.en: I want to drink a glass of cold water, because I am thirsty.

at dø.explanation: "At dø" means "to die". For "have died" Danish uses "er" (am / is), not "har" (have): "Han er død" (He has died).

sentence.da: Planter kan **dø**, hvis de ikke får vand.
sentence.en: Plants can die if they do not get water.

da.explanation: "Da" means "when", for something that happened once in the past. Compare "Da jeg kom hjem, sov børnene" (When I came home, the children were asleep) with "Når jeg kommer hjem, sover børnene" (When I get home, the children are asleep: now or later, not in the past).

sentence.da: **Da** det begyndte at regne, gik vi hjem.
sentence.en: When it began to rain, we went home.

dagens ret.explanation: "Dagens ret" means "dish of the day". Word for word it is "the day's dish": "dagens" (the day's) and "ret" (dish).

sentence.da: Der er mange retter på menuen, men **dagens ret** er fisk.
sentence.en: There are many dishes on the menu, but the dish of the day is fish.

dagligvarer.explanation: "Dagligvarer" means "groceries": everyday goods like food and household things. It is built from "daglig" (daily) and "varer" (goods) and is always plural.

sentence.da: Jeg køber **dagligvarer** i supermarkedet.
sentence.en: I buy groceries at the supermarket.

dansk.explanation: "Dansk" means "Danish", the language and also things from Denmark. As a school subject it is used without "en" or "et": "Jeg har dansk" (I have Danish class). Language names start with a small letter: "dansk" (Danish), "engelsk" (English).

sentence.da: Jeg bor i Danmark, så jeg taler **dansk**.
sentence.en: I live in Denmark, so I speak Danish.

davs.explanation: "Davs" means "hi", a casual greeting for people you know. "Hej" (hi) works with everyone.

sentence.da: **Davs**, Peter! Det er længe siden.
sentence.en: Hi, Peter! It has been a long time.

de.explanation: "De" means "they". Compare "De ser mig" (They see me) with "Jeg ser dem" (I see them), where "dem" means "them". "De" is also "the" before many things: "de store huse" (the big houses).

sentence.da: Anna og Lars er gift, og **de** har to børn.
sentence.en: Anna and Lars are married, and they have two children.

december.explanation: "December" means "December". Danish writes month names with a small letter, so you write "i december" (in December), not "i December".

sentence.da: Vi fejrer jul i **december**.
sentence.en: We celebrate Christmas in December.

dejlig.explanation: "Dejlig" means "lovely" or "nice". It is warmer than "god" (good): "Dejligt!" means "Lovely!".

sentence.da: Solen skinner, og det er en **dejlig** dag.
sentence.en: The sun is shining, and it is a lovely day.

dem.explanation: "Dem" means "them". Compare "De ser mig" (They see me) with "Jeg ser dem" (I see them): "de" (they) is for the ones doing it, "dem" for the ones it happens to.

sentence.da: De er mine naboer, og jeg kan godt lide **dem**.
sentence.en: They are my neighbors, and I like them.

den.explanation: "Den" means "it" for words that take "en". Compare "Jeg har en bil. Den er rød" (I have a car. It is red) with "Jeg har et hus. Det er rødt" (I have a house. It is red). "Den" also means "the" before a describing word: "den store bil" (the big car).

sentence.da: Se på bilen! **Den** er meget stor.
sentence.en: Look at the car! It is very big.

denne.explanation: "Denne" means "this" with words that take "en". Compare "denne bil" (this car) with "dette hus" (this house, as "hus" takes "et"). It sounds formal; in everyday speech people say "den her bil" (this car).

sentence.da: Jeg tager **denne** bil, men ikke den anden.
sentence.en: I am taking this car, but not the other one.

der.explanation: "Der" means "there". Compare "Han er her" (He is here) with "Han er der" (He is there). At the start of a sentence it says something exists: "Der er mange børn" (There are many children). It can also mean "who": "manden, der bor her" (the man who lives here).

sentence.da: **Der** er en kat i haven.
sentence.en: There is a cat in the garden.

derefter.explanation: "Derefter" means "after that". Compare "efter maden" (after the meal) with "derefter" (after that): "Vi ser en film, og derefter går vi i seng" (We watch a film, and after that we go to bed).

sentence.da: Først spiser vi, og **derefter** går vi en tur.
sentence.en: First we eat, and after that we go for a walk.

deres.explanation: "Deres" means "their". Compare "Det er hans hus" (It is his house) with "Det er deres hus" (It is their house). It stays the same for one thing or many: "deres hund" (their dog), "deres hunde" (their dogs).

sentence.da: Peter og Anna bor her. Det er **deres** hus.
sentence.en: Peter and Anna live here. It is their house.

derfor.explanation: "Derfor" means "that is why". The same fact can be said two ways: "Jeg er syg, derfor bliver jeg hjemme" (I am sick, that is why I am staying home) and "Jeg bliver hjemme, fordi jeg er syg" (I am staying home because I am sick).

forms.en: that is why I am here

sentence.da: Det regner, og **derfor** tager jeg en paraply med.
sentence.en: It is raining, and that is why I am taking an umbrella.

derfra.explanation: "Derfra" means "from there". Compare "Jeg kommer herfra" (I come from here) with "Jeg kommer derfra" (I come from there).

forms.en: What can you see from there?

sentence.da: Jeg bor ved havnen. **Derfra** er der kun fem minutter til stationen.
sentence.en: I live by the harbor. From there it is only five minutes to the station.

derhjemme.explanation: "Derhjemme" means "at home", said about your home when you are not in it or about life there in general: "Derhjemme har vi to katte" (At home we have two cats). Compare "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home, right now).

forms.en: what do you do at home?

sentence.da: Vi bor i Danmark, men **derhjemme** taler vi engelsk.
sentence.en: We live in Denmark, but at home we speak English.

derinde.explanation: "Derinde" means "in there". Compare "Jeg er herinde" (I am in here) with "Katten er derinde" (The cat is in there).

forms.en: in there in the living room

sentence.da: Døren er åben, og min mor er **derinde**.
sentence.en: The door is open, and my mother is in there.

dernede.explanation: "Dernede" means "down there". Compare "Katten er deroppe" (The cat is up there) with "Katten er dernede" (The cat is down there).

sentence.da: Jeg står øverst, og bilen står **dernede**.
sentence.en: I am standing at the top, and the car is down there.

derude.explanation: "Derude" means "out there". Compare "Børnene er derinde" (The children are in there) with "Børnene er derude" (The children are out there).

sentence.da: Se ud af vinduet! Børnene leger **derude**.
sentence.en: Look out of the window! The children are playing out there.

desværre.explanation: "Desværre" means "unfortunately". Use it before bad news or a no: "Desværre kan jeg ikke komme" (Unfortunately I can't come). It sounds softer and more polite than just "Nej" (No).

sentence.da: Vil du med i biografen? **Desværre** har jeg ikke tid.
sentence.en: Do you want to come to the cinema? Unfortunately I don't have time.

det.explanation: "Det" means "it" or "that". Use it for a thing that takes "et": "Jeg har et hus, og det er stort" (I have a house, and it is big). Things that take "en" use "den": "Jeg har en bil, og den er stor" (I have a car, and it is big). "Det" is also used for weather and general statements: "Det regner" (It is raining), "Det er sjovt" (That is fun).

forms.en: I know it / I know that.

sentence.da: Se på huset! **Det** er meget gammelt.
sentence.en: Look at the house! It is very old.

det er.explanation: "Det er" means "it is" or "that is"; Danish uses the same two words for both. Use it to name things or describe them: "Det er sent" (It is late).

sentence.da: **Det er** en god dag i dag.
sentence.en: It is a good day today.

det er en god idé.explanation: "Det er en god idé" means "that's a good idea", said to agree with a suggestion. In everyday talk Danes often shorten it to "god idé!" (good idea!).

sentence.da: Skal vi tage på café? **Det er en god idé.**
sentence.en: Shall we go to a cafe? That's a good idea.

det er i orden.explanation: "Det er i orden" means "it's okay" or "that's fine". Danes say it in reply to "undskyld" (sorry) and to agree to a plan. "I orden" literally means "in order". Ask "er det i orden?" (is that okay?) to check if something suits the other person.

sentence.da: Undskyld, jeg er sent på den. — **Det er i orden.**
sentence.en: Sorry, I'm late. — It's okay.

det er ikke så svært.explanation: "Det er ikke så svært" means "it's not that hard". "Svært" means "difficult" and "ikke så" means "not so".

sentence.da: Dansk? **Det er ikke så svært.**
sentence.en: Danish? It's not that hard.

det er lige meget.explanation: "Det er lige meget" means "it doesn't matter". Use it when you are happy with any choice. Careful with tone: "Det er mig lige meget" (I don't care) can sound rude, so say "det gør ikke noget" (it's no problem) when you want to be kind.

forms.da: Det er lige meget, hvad du vælger.
forms.en: It doesn't matter what you choose.

sentence.da: **Det er lige meget**, jeg tager hvad som helst.
sentence.en: It doesn't matter, I'll take anything.

det er rigtigt.explanation: "Det er rigtigt" means "that's right". Be careful: "rigtig" also means "really" before another word, as in "rigtig godt" (really good).

sentence.da: Du bor i Aarhus, ikke? **Det er rigtigt.**
sentence.en: You live in Aarhus, right? That's right.

det er synd.explanation: "Det er synd" means "that's a shame" or "that's too bad", and shows sympathy when something goes wrong. To say you feel sorry for someone, add "for" and the person: "Det er synd for ham" (I feel sorry for him).

sentence.da: Du kan ikke komme? **Det er synd!**
sentence.en: You can't come? That's a shame!

det går fint.explanation: "Det går fint" means "it's going fine" and is a common answer to "Hvordan går det?" (How is it going?). Swap "fint" (fine) for "godt" (well) or "dårligt" (badly) to change the mood.

sentence.da: Hvordan går det? **Det går fint**, tak.
sentence.en: How is it going? It's going fine, thanks.

det går godt.explanation: "Det går godt" means "it's going well" and is a standard answer to "Hvordan går det?" (How's it going?). After answering, it is polite to ask "og dig?" (and you?).

sentence.da: Hvordan går det? **Det går godt**, tak.
sentence.en: How's it going? It's going well, thanks.

det gør ikke noget.explanation: "Det gør ikke noget" means "it's ok" or "no problem", what you say when someone says "Undskyld" (Sorry). Word for word it is "it does not do anything". Do not mix it up with "det er lige meget" (it doesn't matter), which is for choices.

forms.da: Det gør ikke noget, jeg venter.

sentence.da: "Undskyld!" – "**Det gør ikke noget.**"
sentence.en: "Sorry!" – "It's ok."

det håber jeg.explanation: "Det håber jeg" means "I hope so", a short reply to a question about something that might happen. Word for word it is "that hope I".

sentence.da: Bliver det godt vejr? **Det håber jeg.**
sentence.en: Will the weather be good? I hope so.

det lyder godt.explanation: "Det lyder godt" means "that sounds good". Use it to react positively to a plan, an offer or an idea. "At lyde" means "to sound".

sentence.da: Skal vi spise middag klokken seks? **Det lyder godt.**
sentence.en: Shall we have dinner at six? That sounds good.

det tror jeg.explanation: "Det tror jeg" means "I think so" or "I believe so", a slightly unsure reply when you aren't completely certain. Word for word it is "that think I".

sentence.da: Er han hjemme? **Det tror jeg.**
sentence.en: Is he home? I think so.

det tror jeg ikke.explanation: "Det tror jeg ikke" means "I don't think so", a soft way to say no. Word for word it is "that think I not". It sounds gentler than a plain "nej" (no).

sentence.da: **Det tror jeg ikke**, men jeg er ikke sikker.
sentence.en: I don't think so, but I'm not sure.

det var så lidt.explanation: "Det var så lidt" means "you're welcome" or "don't mention it". Word for word it is "it was so little", as if the favour was nothing. It is a warm, slightly informal answer to "tak" (thanks).

forms.da: Tak for hjælpen! – Det var så lidt.
forms.en: Thanks for the help! – Don't mention it.

sentence.da: Tusind tak for hjælpen! – **Det var så lidt.**
sentence.en: A thousand thanks for the help! – Don't mention it.

det ved jeg ikke.explanation: "Det ved jeg ikke" means "I don't know". "Det" (that) comes first, then "ved jeg" (know I). "At vide" (to know) is for facts; for knowing a person or place use "at kende" (to know).

forms.da: Det ved jeg ikke noget om.

sentence.da: **Det ved jeg ikke**, men jeg kan spørge.
sentence.en: I don't know, but I can ask.

dette.explanation: "Dette" means "this" with a word that takes "et": "dette hus" (this house). With a word that takes "en", use "denne": "denne bil" (this car). It sounds a bit formal; in everyday speech Danes say "det her": "Jeg vil have det her" (I want this one).

sentence.da: Jeg vil købe **dette** hus, men ikke det andet.
sentence.en: I want to buy this house, but not the other one.

dig.explanation: "Dig" means "you" when something is done to you: "Jeg elsker dig" (I love you). "Du" is the one who does it: "Du elsker mig" (You love me). It is also used after little words like "med" (with): "Jeg kommer med dig" (I am coming with you). It is for one person; for several people say "jer" (you, many).

sentence.da: Jeg kan høre **dig**.
sentence.en: I can hear you.

digital.explanation: "Digital" means "digital". It looks like the English word, but the stress is on the last part: di-gi-TAL.

sentence.da: Klokken har ingen visere, kun tal. Det er en **digital** klokke.
sentence.en: The clock has no hands, only numbers. It is a digital clock.

din.explanation: "Din" means "your" or "yours" when you talk to one person and the thing takes "en": "din bil" (your car). For a thing that takes "et" it is "dit": "dit hus" (your house). For more than one thing it is "dine": "dine sko" (your shoes).

sentence.da: Her er **din** kaffe, værsgo.
sentence.en: Here is your coffee, here you go.

dine.explanation: "Dine" means "your" or "yours" when there is more than one thing: "dine sko" (your shoes). For one thing it is "din" or "dit": "din sko" (your shoe), "dit hus" (your house). It is also used on its own: "Skoene er dine" (The shoes are yours).

sentence.da: Tag **dine** sko på, vi skal ud.
sentence.en: Put your shoes on, we are going out.

disse.explanation: "Disse" means "these": "disse sko" (these shoes). For one thing it is "denne" or "dette": "denne sko" (this shoe), "dette hus" (this house). It sounds a bit formal; in everyday speech Danes say "de her": "de her sko" (these shoes).

sentence.da: Kig på **disse** to biler: de er begge røde.
sentence.en: Look at these two cars: they are both red.

dit.explanation: "Dit" means "your" or "yours" when you talk to one person and the thing takes "et": "dit hus" (your house), "dit navn" (your name). For a thing that takes "en" it is "din": "din bil" (your car). For more than one thing it is "dine": "dine sko" (your shoes).

sentence.da: Hvad er **dit** navn?
sentence.en: What is your name?

dog.explanation: "Dog" means "though", "still" or "anyway". It adds a little contrast: "Det er dyrt, men jeg køber det dog" (It is expensive, but I am buying it anyway). In a command it makes the request friendlier: "Kom dog ind!" (Do come in!). It is not the same as "men" (but): "Han er sød, men sur" (He is sweet but grumpy).

sentence.da: Jeg er træt, men jeg kommer **dog**.
sentence.en: I am tired, but I am coming anyway.

du.explanation: "Du" means "you" when you talk to one person: "Du er sød" (You are sweet). Danes use it with almost everyone, even older people and your boss. When something is done to you, it is "dig": "Jeg ser dig" (I see you). When you talk to several people, say "I": "I er søde" (You are all sweet).

sentence.da: Hvor bor **du**?
sentence.en: Where do you live?

dum.explanation: "Dum" means "stupid" or "silly". Said about a person it can sound rude: "Du er dum" (You are stupid). About things it is milder: "Det var dumt" (That was silly).

sentence.da: Det var en **dum** fejl.
sentence.en: That was a stupid mistake.

dyb.explanation: "Dyb" means "deep", as in deep water or a deep hole. It also works for sleep and voices: "en dyb søvn" (a deep sleep), "en dyb stemme" (a deep voice).

sentence.da: Man kan ikke stå op i vandet, for søen er meget **dyb**.
sentence.en: You cannot stand up in the water, because the lake is very deep.

dyr.explanation: "Dyr" means "expensive", as in "Det er for dyrt" (It is too expensive). Be careful: "et dyr" is also a word of its own meaning "an animal".

sentence.da: Jakken koster 5000 kroner. Den er meget **dyr**.
sentence.en: The jacket costs 5000 kroner. It is very expensive.

dårlig.explanation: "Dårlig" means "bad", and it also means "unwell": "Jeg har det dårligt" means "I feel bad" or "I feel ill". Its "worse" and "worst" are different words: "værre" (worse) and "værst" (worst).

sentence.da: Jeg tabte alle pengene. Det var en **dårlig** idé.
sentence.en: I lost all the money. It was a bad idea.

død.explanation: "Død" means "dead", for people, animals and plants. It is also used for things that have stopped working: "Min telefon er død" (My phone is dead).

sentence.da: Blomsten har ikke fået vand i en måned, nu er den **død**.
sentence.en: The flower has not had water for a month, now it is dead.

en dag.explanation: "En dag" means "a day", as in "hver dag" (every day) and "god dag" (hello, good day). The days of the week end in "-dag", for example "mandag" (Monday) and "tirsdag" (Tuesday).

sentence.da: Mandag er den første **dag** i ugen.
sentence.en: Monday is the first day of the week.

en dame.explanation: "En dame" means "a lady", a polite word for a woman. You often see "Damer" on a toilet door, meaning the women's toilet. "Mine damer og herrer" means "Ladies and gentlemen".

sentence.da: Den **dame** i den smukke kjole er min tante.
sentence.en: The lady in the beautiful dress is my aunt.

en dansker.explanation: "En dansker" means "a Dane", a person from Denmark. The word is the same for men and women. To say what nationality someone is, Danish leaves out "en": "Han er dansker" means "He is a Dane".

sentence.da: Han bor i Danmark og er **dansker**.
sentence.en: He lives in Denmark and is a Dane.

en dato.explanation: "En dato" means "a date" on the calendar, such as 5 March. Use it to ask: "Hvad er datoen i dag?" (What is the date today?). Do not mix it up with a romantic date, which is "en date" (borrowed from English).

sentence.da: Hvilken **dato** er det i dag? Det er den femte marts.
sentence.en: What date is it today? It is the fifth of March.

sentence.da: Min søn er en dreng, og min **datter** er en pige.
sentence.en: My son is a boy, and my daughter is a girl.

en dessert.explanation: "En dessert" means "a dessert", the sweet dish at the end of a meal. It is spelled like the English word, but the stress is at the end: "des-SERT".

sentence.da: Efter maden vil jeg gerne have en **dessert**, for eksempel is.
sentence.en: After the meal I would like a dessert, for example ice cream.

en doktor.explanation: "En doktor" means "a doctor", but in everyday Danish people mostly say "en læge" (a medical doctor). Still, "Jeg skal til doktoren" (I am going to the doctor) is fine in casual speech.

sentence.da: Jeg skal til **doktor** Hansen, fordi jeg er syg.
sentence.en: I am going to Doctor Hansen because I am sick.

en dollar.explanation: "En dollar" means "a dollar". Danish money is "kroner" (crowns), not dollars.

sentence.da: Det koster ti **dollar**.
sentence.en: It costs ten dollars.

en dreng.explanation: "En dreng" means "a boy", a young male child. For a young adult, say "en ung mand" (a young man).

sentence.da: Den lille **dreng** leger med sin bil, og pigen leger med sin dukke.
sentence.en: The little boy plays with his car, and the girl plays with her doll.

en drik.explanation: "En drik" means "a drink", from "at drikke" (to drink). In everyday speech people usually name the drink itself, like "en kaffe" (a coffee) or "en øl" (a beer).

sentence.da: Jeg er tørstig. Må jeg få en kold **drik**?
sentence.en: I am thirsty. May I have a cold drink?

en dukke.explanation: "En dukke" means "a doll", a toy for children. A puppet in a show is also "en dukke", and "dukketeater" means "puppet theatre".

sentence.da: Pigen leger med sin **dukke**.
sentence.en: The girl is playing with her doll.

en dør.explanation: "En dør" means "a door". Common phrases are "at åbne døren" (to open the door) and "at lukke døren" (to close the door). The letter "ø" sounds a bit like the "u" in "fur".

sentence.da: Jeg åbner en **dør** og går ind i huset.
sentence.en: I open a door and go into the house.

et dankort.explanation: "Et dankort" means "a Dankort", the Danish debit card. To ask if a shop takes it, say "Kan jeg betale med dankort?" (Can I pay by Dankort?). Note that Danish leaves out "a" after "med" here.

sentence.da: Jeg har ingen kontanter, så jeg betaler med **dankort**.
sentence.en: I have no cash, so I pay with a Dankort.

et dobbeltværelse.explanation: "Et dobbeltværelse" means "a double room", a hotel room for two people. It is made of "dobbelt" (double) and "et værelse" (a room).

sentence.da: Vi er to personer, så vi vil gerne have et **dobbeltværelse**.
sentence.en: There are two of us, so we would like a double room.

et dyr.explanation: "Et dyr" means "an animal". "Et vildt dyr" means "a wild animal".

sentence.da: Hunde, katte og fugle er **dyr**.
sentence.en: Dogs, cats and birds are animals.
